name: Add lesson resource
description: Instructor is editing a course lesson in the curriculum editor (desktop, logged-in instructor). The entry point is an open lesson ('Understanding A1 to B1 CEFR Levels') in the course curriculum. The happy path: instructor opens the lesson, clicks Add content, chooses the Resource content type, uploads or imports a file via the Add resource modal, confirms the upload, and returns to the lesson with the resource attached and a visible download link. Exit point: the lesson editor showing the newly added resource beneath the lesson content. Assumptions: user is authenticated with course-edit permissions, using a desktop browser, and file-upload/import integrations (local device, link, Dropbox, Google Drive) are available.
problem:
User task (user perspective): Attach a downloadable resource file (e.g., a .docx) to a specific lesson so students can download it. The user expects to find an 'Add content' control, select the relevant content type, supply a file (drag/drop, browse, or import), confirm upload, and then see the file listed in the lesson with a download link visible.

Interface/system perspective: The UI exposes an 'Add content' action inside a lesson editor which opens a content picker. Selecting 'Resource' opens a modal for file input with multiple import sources and drag/drop support. The system accepts the selected file, shows a preview in the modal, provides an explicit upload/confirm control, and upon successful upload the editor injects a new Resource block under the lesson content and marks the download link as visible. 

Result at end: User-perceived outcome — the file appears in the lesson as a Resource block (e.g., 'Introduction.docx') with a label indicating the download link is visible. System-level outcome — the resource file is stored and associated with the lesson so students can access/download it when the lesson is published or visible to them.

content.description:
The screen is a web-based curriculum management interface for an online education platform named 'Liam's School'. The design adopts a clean, minimalistic layout with a predominantly white background (#FFFFFF) for the main content area and a dark sidebar (#2E2E2E) on the left side. The left vertical sidebar includes navigation links with white (#FFFFFF) text and some accent highlights in bright yellow (#FFD700), such as the "Setup guide" button and the selected course title. The sidebar uses simple icons in white and has the user's name 'Liam' at the bottom. The main content area is split horizontally into multiple sections with clear separation.

At the top, breadcrumb navigation is included in small, light gray (#6E6E6E) font for context. The page heading uses a serif or classic font in black (#000000) at a large size (around 24-28px) for "Curriculum".

The main content block is a white card with subtle gray borders (#CCCCCC) and rounded corners, containing a section header "Understanding A1 to B1 CEFR Levels" with a "Publish" button styled as a rectangular button with a subtle border and black text. Adjacent is an "Edit" link.

The main text area within this block contains a block of lesson description text with normal body font style (approximately 14-16px, line height 1.5, dark gray #333333). Bullet points highlight key lesson concepts.

Below the main content are lesson settings with toggle switches for "Student comments" and "Public preview" states, styled as circular toggles in gray with an X mark indicating off state. A red delete link "Delete lesson" is positioned below these toggles.

On the right side, a narrow vertical outline panel presents an "Outline" with headings and sub-items, the text is dark gray with a small "Edit" link in blue. The outline is categorized into sections such as Introduction, Building Foundations, Speaking Skills Development.

A prominent bright yellow (#FFD700) "Preview" button is located at the top right area, ensuring user focus and easy access.

The layout is spacious with generous padding around elements for clarity and readability. Typography is consistent with sans-serif fonts for body and controls, and serif or bold for headings.

Overall, the style is professional and functional designed for course authors to create, manage and preview curriculum steps efficiently. The interface is user-friendly, with clear call-to-actions and a logical hierarchy, combining navigation, content editing, and settings on a single screen.
content.layout:
The screen uses a two main column layout: a fixed vertical left sidebar and a flexible main content area that includes two primary horizontal sections. The sidebar on the left is a vertical navigation pane occupying approximately 20% of the screen width, with stacked navigation items arranged vertically, each spaced with padding for comfortable touch/click targets. The sidebar includes a footer area at the bottom with the account name.

The main content area (about 80% width) is divided horizontally into two main parts. The top horizontal section contains the breadcrumb navigation at the very top, followed by the large main curriculum content card aligned center-left, which takes about 60% of the horizontal space. Adjacent to this, on the right, is a narrower vertical outline panel (around 25% width), with the outline title, list of course sections and lesson titles arranged vertically in a scrollable container with spacing between items.

Below the main content card, there is a settings section with toggles and action buttons arranged vertically. All content sections use consistent padding and margins, with alignment primarily left-aligned for text blocks and controls, creating a balanced and readable structure.

The layout keywords are: two-column, vertical sidebar, horizontal section division, card layout, vertical list, fixed navigation, responsive spacing, vertical alignment, scrollable outline, toggle controls.
content.functions:
Users can review and manage the curriculum of an online educational course. Specifically, they can read the lesson content and key concepts presented within a text block that includes paragraphs and bullet points. Users have the ability to edit the text and images of the lesson by clicking the 'Edit' link, which likely transforms the content area into an editable form. Authors can publish the lesson content using the 'Publish' button to make it available to students and set its live status.

On the right, users can view and interact with the course outline that shows different course sections and lessons, helping them navigate and manage the curriculum structure. An 'Edit' link near the outline enables modification of the outline content.

In the lower area, users can toggle lesson settings such as enabling or disabling student comments and public previews to control interactions and visibility of the lesson content. They also have the option to delete the lesson entirely via a clearly marked 'Delete lesson' button.

At the top right corner, a 'Preview' button allows users to see how the course or specific lesson would appear to learners. This facilitates checking the final rendered version before publishing or making further changes.

Together, these features enable course creators to build, edit, organize, and control their educational content efficiently in a single interface, supporting the broader goal of managing and delivering online courses effectively.

Beneath the drop zone is a light beige horizontal information bar containing a small lightning bolt icon on the left and text describing a limitation: 'This plan is limited to 10 lesson video uploads, and video resources count toward that limit.
